title: The Evening Brief: Playoffs arrive, injuries pile up, Ovechkin bows out
dek: Baseball's first round is under way with dramatic finishes, football's injury reports are mounting across the league, and the NHL's greatest goal-scorer announced his farewell season on Monday.
author: GoCheckMySports
bottom_line: The Rays and Brewers each won their first NLDS or ALDS games behind elite pitching performances; the Cowboys mounted a 10-point halftime comeback on a historic receiving night by Lamb; the Ravens won but lost their reigning MVP to an ankle injury now listed day-to-day; the Seahawks signed Joe Mixon to the practice squad after a 2025 absence; the Packers await final evaluation on Edgerrin Cooper's Achilles injury; and Ovechkin announced the 2026-27 season will be his last in the NHL. The coming days will test whether Jackson can return for Cincinnati on October 10, whether Tampa Bay and Milwaukee can win their next games, and whether Mixon can contribute meaningfully after his extended absence from competition.
body: The postseason arrived in baseball on October 4 with two dominant pitching performances that set the tone for their series. Drew Rasmussen carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning with 10 strikeouts as the Tampa Bay Rays defeated the New York Yankees 1-0 in ALDS Game 1. Rasmussen retired 15 straight batters and recorded 23 swinging strikes, a career-high and the most by a Ray in a postseason game. Austin Wells broke the no-hit bid with a double in the eighth but was thrown out at third. Jonathan Aranda's third-inning home run provided the only run. In Milwaukee, Jackson Chourio delivered a two-out, two-strike single in the bottom of the ninth to lift the Brewers past the San Diego Padres 4-3 in NLDS Game 2, extending the series lead to 2-0. The hit scored Christian Yelich and Sal Frelick and marked the first last-inning comeback in Brewers postseason history that began with Milwaukee trailing. Mason Miller, the Padres' elite closer, allowed the single after the team had entered the ninth leading 3-2.

In the NFL, Sunday brought a historic offensive performance and a significant injury. CeeDee Lamb caught a career-high 17 passes for 189 yards, including a game-winning 12-yard touchdown with 40 seconds remaining, as the Dallas Cowboys defeated the Houston Texans 34-30 after trailing 16-6 at halftime. Lamb's 17 catches mark the most in a single game by a wide receiver in Cowboys history; only Jason Witten, a tight end, has caught more in a Cowboys game (18 in 2012). Lamb was targeted on 21 of 45 routes, the most targets by any receiver running 45 or fewer routes in a single game since the Next Gen Stats era began in 2016. Dallas scored touchdowns on four of five second-half possessions to complete the comeback. The Ravens' victory over Tennessee came at a cost: Lamar Jackson left the game with an ankle injury late in the first half on the second-to-last play before halftime after a sack by Jermaine Johnson II and did not return. Head coach Jesse Minter said the team does not yet know the extent of the injury. NFL Network reports Jackson is day-to-day. Tyler Huntley took over at quarterback to begin the second half in Baltimore's 24-18 win.

Injuries continued to mount across football on Sunday and Monday. The Packers suspect linebacker Edgerrin Cooper's non-contact Achilles injury, suffered in the third quarter against Tampa Bay, will end his season, though final evaluation is ongoing. Isaiah McDuffie replaced Cooper at linebacker. The Seahawks signed running back Joe Mixon to their practice squad on Monday after hosting him for a workout. Mixon, a two-time Pro Bowler, missed the entire 2025 season due to a foot injury but posted 1,325 scrimmage yards and 12 touchdowns in 2024 with Houston. Seattle's move comes amid depth concerns at the position, with Zach Charbonnet's practice window activated and Jadarian Price on injured reserve with a chest injury.

On the hockey calendar, Alexander Ovechkin announced on Monday, October 5 that the 2026-27 season will be his 22nd and final year in the NHL. Ovechkin, the league's all-time leading goal-scorer with 929 career goals, told his Washington Capitals teammates in a video message: "This is gonna be my last year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun." The Capitals have reinforced the roster with trades and free-agent signings to support one final Stanley Cup push.

The thread across the day is the collision of extremes: two pitchers dominant enough to carry no-hitters into the late innings, a receiver on pace for record-breaking yardage against a historic target volume, a reigning MVP sidelined by a single play, and a transcendent goal-scorer entering his final chapter. What binds them is the clarity they carry: the Rays and Brewers know who they are right now; Lamb and the Cowboys know what they can do in the right moments; Ovechkin knows when to step away.
